# Reproducibility and code as an output

A paper makes a claim; reproducibility is whether anyone can check it. The standard to aim for is that your results are a function of your data and your code (`results = f(data, code)`), and that a stranger with both can run one command and get your numbers, figures, and tables back. The open-science chapter covered the *policy*: preregister, share data, share code. This chapter covers the *practice* that makes shared code worth sharing, and treats the code and data themselves as research outputs that get cited, licensed, and archived like the paper.

The reason to care is not virtue. The datasets behind most papers become unavailable within a few years, and analysis code that ran once on its author's laptop rarely runs anywhere else. Reproducibility is the discipline that stops your own results becoming irretrievable to you: the version of "future you" who, eighteen months from now, gets a reviewer asking for one more sensitivity analysis and cannot rerun the pipeline [@sandve2013reproducible].

## Pin the environment

Code does not run in a vacuum; it runs against specific versions of specific packages, and those change. A script that gives one answer today can give another, or none, when a dependency updates. Record the environment so it can be rebuilt.

- **R:** `renv::init()` at the start of a project and `renv::snapshot()` when you publish writes an `renv.lock` file naming every package and its exact version. A collaborator runs `renv::restore()` and gets your library.
- **Python:** a virtual environment (`venv` or conda) plus a pinned `requirements.txt` (`pip freeze > requirements.txt`) or an `environment.yml`. Pin versions (`pandas==2.2.1`), not just names.
- **Either, for full isolation:** a container. A `Dockerfile` captures the operating system, the language runtime, and the packages, so the analysis runs identically on any machine and will still run in five years. Reach for it when the stack is complex or the result is high-stakes; for a single R project, `renv` is usually enough.

At minimum, end an R script with `sessionInfo()` and a Python one with the pinned requirements file. A reader who knows your package versions can reconstruct your environment; one who does not is guessing.

## Make it deterministic

An analysis that uses randomness (a train/validation split, a bootstrap, multiple imputation, a permutation test) gives a different answer every run unless you fix the seed. Set it once, at the top, and the run becomes repeatable.

The cohorts in this book are the worked example: [`figures/sw_cohort.py`](https://github.com/tiagojct/working-draft/blob/main/figures/sw_cohort.py) sets `SEED = 20260515` and draws from `numpy.random.default_rng(SEED)`, so the committed dataset is the same every time the script runs. In R, `set.seed()` before the random step does the same. Seed discipline is what separates "reproducible" from "reproducible except for the numbers that move", and reviewers notice when a bootstrap CI changes between the manuscript and the revision.

One caveat worth stating in the methods: a fixed seed makes a result *repeatable* (same code, same numbers), not *robust* (the finding survives a different seed). Report that the seed was fixed; do not present a single lucky draw as if the seed did not matter.

## Structure the project so it runs itself

A reproducible project has an obvious layout and a single entry point.

```
project/
  data/raw/        # inputs, never edited by hand
  data/derived/    # everything here is regenerated by code
  R/  or  src/     # analysis scripts, numbered or a pipeline
  figures/         # outputs, regenerated
  manuscript.qmd   # the paper
  renv.lock        # or requirements.txt
  README.md        # how to run it, in order
```

The rule that makes this work: **nothing in `derived/` or `figures/` is ever edited by hand**; it is all output, regenerated from `raw/` by code. If you fix a number in a figure by opening it in an editor, the figure and the code have diverged and the project is no longer reproducible. Build automation enforces this: `targets` (R) or a `Makefile` expresses the dependency graph so that `make` (or `targets::tar_make()`) rebuilds only what changed and guarantees the outputs match the current code. This book is itself an instance: every figure is regenerated by [`figures/generate.py`](https://github.com/tiagojct/working-draft/blob/main/figures/generate.py), never touched by hand.

## Version-control the code, not just the manuscript

The co-authorship chapter used Git to track manuscript drafts. Its more important job is tracking analysis code. Put the project in a Git repository from the first script, commit in small logical steps with messages that say *why*, and you get a complete, dated history of every analytic decision, invaluable when a reviewer asks why you changed a covariate three months ago.

Two rules specific to clinical code:

- **Never commit patient data.** A `.gitignore` that excludes `data/raw/`, `*.csv` with real values, and anything under a controlled-access agreement keeps protected health information out of the history, where, once committed and pushed, it is very hard to remove. Commit the *code* and a *synthetic* or de-identified sample, never the real records.
- **Tag the release.** When the paper is submitted, tag the exact commit (`git tag v1.0-submission`) so the code that produced the reported results is recoverable even as the repository moves on.

A public GitHub repository is not an archive: repositories are deleted, made private, or rewritten. Archive the tagged release to a DOI-issuing repository (open science chapter) so the citable version is permanent.

## Code and data are citable outputs

Your analysis code and your dataset are research products in their own right. Treat them as citable.

- **Cite the software you used.** `citation("lme4")` in R and a package's `CITATION.cff` file give the reference the authors ask for; naming and versioning the tools that produced your results is both courteous and part of reproducibility. "Analyses used R 4.4.1 and the `survival` package (v3.7)" belongs in the methods.
- **Licence what you release.** Code with no licence is, legally, code no one may reuse. A permissive licence (MIT, Apache-2.0) for code and an open licence (CC BY) for data and text tell readers what they may do. State the licence in the repository and the data-availability statement.
- **Consider a software or data paper.** A genuinely reusable tool or dataset can be published in its own right (*JOSS* for software, *Scientific Data* or *Data in Brief* for datasets), giving it a citable DOI and formal credit separate from the analysis paper [@smith2016software].

## Manage the data as data

Sharing a CSV is not data management. The FAIR principles (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) are the standard funders increasingly expect, and they are mostly about metadata [@wilkinson2016fair]. Two artifacts do most of the work:

- **A data dictionary** (codebook): one row per variable, with its name, type, units, coding, and allowed range. Without it, a shared dataset is a grid of numbers no one else can interpret; with it, a reader knows that `nyha_admission` is a factor with levels I–IV and that `egfr` is in mL/min/1.73m².
- **A de-identification step, documented.** Clinical data cannot be shared until direct identifiers are removed. The HIPAA Safe Harbor method names eighteen identifier types to strip; k-anonymity ensures no combination of quasi-identifiers (age, postcode, admission date) picks out fewer than *k* individuals. When even a de-identified release is too risky, generate a **synthetic** dataset that preserves the analytic structure without exposing anyone (open science chapter). This book's cohorts are exactly that.

## Write the paper as an executable document

The strongest form of reproducibility folds the analysis into the manuscript: a Quarto (`.qmd`) or R Markdown (`.Rmd`) document that runs from raw data to every figure, table, and in-text number the paper reports. Nothing is copied by hand, so nothing can be transcribed wrong, and the whole paper rebuilds with one command. This book is written that way. Notebooks (Jupyter) can do the same but carry a caveat: their cells can be run out of order, so a notebook that "works" interactively may not run top-to-bottom: always restart and run-all before trusting one, and export a script or a rendered document as the reproducible artifact.

## Practice: make this analysis reproducible

A collaborator sends you a folder: `analysis_final_v3.R`, `data.csv` (the real patient export), and `Figure2_edited.png`. Name three things wrong with this as a reproducible project, before revealing the answer.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer

1. **Real patient data in the shareable folder, and presumably in version control.** `data.csv` with real values should never be committed or shared; it needs de-identification or a synthetic stand-in, and a `.gitignore` to keep it out of the repository history.
2. **A hand-edited figure.** `Figure2_edited.png` was opened and changed by hand, so it no longer matches any code, and the figure and the analysis have diverged. Figures must be regenerated from the script, never retouched.
3. **No environment and a fragile name.** `_final_v3` is version control by filename (the thing Git exists to replace), and there is no `renv.lock`/`requirements.txt` or `sessionInfo()`, so the packages the script needs are unknown. A stranger cannot rebuild the environment or trust that the script still runs.
:::
